# 3.  Duplicate rows
#       * duplicated() returns TRUE for each row that is an exact copy of an             earlier row. Summing those TRUEs counts the duplicates, because TRUE           counts as 1.
#        * distinct() (from dplyr) keeps only unique rows

```{r}
# Count fully duplicated rows
duplicate_count <- sum(duplicated(world_population))
cat("Duplicated rows found: ", duplicate_count, "\n")

# Keep only unique rows (does nothing if the count above is 0)
world_population <- distinct(world_population)

# Confirm the new shape
dim(world_population)
```

# 7.  Count the outliers

```{r}
# Count values outside the 1.5 IQR fences for one numeric vector
count_outliers <- function(x){
  quartiles <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr_value <- quartiles[2] - quartiles[1]
  lower_fence <- quartiles[1] - 1.5 * iqr_value
  upper_fence <- quartiles[2] + 1.5 * iqr_value
  sum(x < lower_fence | x > upper_fence, na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Apply to every quantitative column
sapply(quantitative_data, count_outliers)
```

```{r}
# Define the time frame once, so it is easy to change and clear to read
base_year         <- 2022
projection_year   <- 2030
years_ahead       <- projection_year - base_year   # t = 8

# Sanity check: all multipliers must be > 0 for log() to work
summary(world_population$`Growth Rate`)
```

 *** log(): the natural logarithm (base e) in R. It convertss a yearly multipliers such as 1.0257 into the continuous rate r
 *** exp(x): computes e^x
 *** mutate(): adds new columns without changing the existing ones
 *** round(): people come in whole numbers
 
```{r}
# Add the continuous growth rate and the 2030 projection as new columns
world_population <- world_population %>%
  mutate(
    # r: continuous growth rate; e^r = Growth Rate, so r = ln(Growth Rate)
    growth_rate_r = log(`Growth Rate`),
    
    # Nt = P * e^(r * t)
    population_30 = round(`2022 Population` * exp(growth_rate_r * years_ahead))
  )
```
 
```{r}
# Top 10 most populous contries: 2022 versus projected 2030
world_population %>%
  arrange(desc(`2022 Population`)) %>%
  select(`Country/Territory`, `2022 Population`, `Growth Rate`, growth_rate_r, population_30) %>%
  head(10)
```

### Step 4.4, Plot 3: CO2 emission trend of the top 10
#  1. Clean the duplicated 2019 column

We noted earlier that 2019...34 and 2019...35 looked identical. We check that before dropping one, instead of assuming.

```{r}

identical(co2_emisions$`2019...34`, co2_emisions$`2019...35`)
```

```{r}

co2_emisions <- co2_emisions %>%
  select(-`2019...35`) %>%
```

### 2. Match countries using codes, instead of names

Names can differ between datasets (for example “Russia” vs “Russian Federation”), but the 3-letter code is the same. The population data calls it CCA3 and the CO2 data calls it country_code.

```{r}
# Codes of the top 10 countries
top10_codes <- top10_countries$CCA3

# Keep only those countries in the CO2 data
co2_top10 <- co2_emisions %>%
  filter(country_code %in% top10_codes)

# Checks: expect 10 rows and no missing codes
nrow(co2_top10)
setdiff(top10_codes, co2_emisions$country_code)
```

```{r}
# Reshape to long format and add consistent country names
co2_top10_long <- co2_top10 %>%
  select(country_code, `1990`:`2019`) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols      = `1990`:`2019`,
               names_to  = "year",
               values_to = "co2_per_capita") %>%   # corrected spelling
  mutate(year = as.integer(year)) %>%
  # Attach the country names used in the population dataset
  left_join(select(top10_countries, CCA3, `Country/Territory`),
            by = c("country_code" = "CCA3"))

# Confirm the column names before plotting
names(co2_top10_long)
```

### Step 4.5, part 1: Correlation between Area, Density, Growth Rate and World Population Percentage

*** cor() computes correlations. method = "pearson" measures linear relationships and "spearman" measures rank-based ones, which are less affected by outliers (we kept those, so we use both).
*** use = "complete.obs" skips rows with NA values (there are none, but it’s a good habit).


```{r}
# Select the four variables named in the work
corr_data <- world_population %>%
  select(area_km2, density_km2, `Growth Rate`, `World Population Percentage`)

# Correlation matrices: Pearson (linear) and Spearman (rank-based)
cor_pearson <- cor(corr_data, method = "pearson", use = "complete.obs")
cor_spearman <- cor(corr_data, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")

round(cor_pearson, 3)
round(cor_spearman, 3)
```

```{r}

# Convert the Pearson matrix to long format for ggplot2
cor_long <- as.data.frame(cor_pearson) %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "variable_1") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -variable_1,
               names_to = "variable_2",
               values_to = "correlation")


# Heatmap: colour shows the strength and direction, the number is printed in each tile
ggplot(cor_long,
       aes(x = variable_1,
           y = variable_2,
           fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(
    label = round(correlation, 2)
  )) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "firebrick", mid = "white", high = "steelblue",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation heatmap (Pearson)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```
### Reading the Pearson matrix (heatmap)

Almost everything is near zero, except one pair:

    * Area vs World Population Percentage: 0.453, a moderate positive relationship.
    * Everything else is between -0.07 and -0.01, so there is essentially no linear               relationship.

Taken alone, this would suggest Area, Density and Growth Rate are unrelated. That conclusion would be wrong.

### Fixing the heatmap (small but worth doing)

The heatmap is correct, but I’d improve two things for the report: the axis order is mixed (x runs one way, y the other), and it only shows Pearson. Since Spearman is the more reliable one here, plot both. This version fixes the order and shows both side by side:

```{r}
# Helper: convert a correlation matrix to long format and label the method
make_cor_long <- function(cor_matrix, method_name) {
  as.data.frame(cor_matrix) %>%
    rownames_to_column(var = "variable_1") %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = -variable_1,
                 names_to = "variable_2",
                 values_to = "correlation") %>%
    mutate(method = method_name)
}

# Combine both methods into one table
cor_both <- bind_rows(
  make_cor_long(cor_pearson,  "Pearson"),
  make_cor_long(cor_spearman, "Spearman")
)

# Fix the order of the variables so both axes match
var_order <- colnames(cor_pearson)
cor_both <- cor_both %>%
  mutate(variable_1 = factor(variable_1, levels = var_order),
         variable_2 = factor(variable_2, levels = rev(var_order)))

# Heatmaps side by side
ggplot(cor_both, aes(x = variable_1, y = variable_2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(correlation, 2))) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "firebrick", mid = "white", high = "steelblue",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  labs(title = "Correlation heatmaps: Pearson vs Spearman",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```
### Report log: Step 4.5, part 1
      * Pearson: only Area vs World Population Percentage is notable (0.453); all other            pairs are about zero (|r| ≤ 0.07).
      * Spearman reveals much stronger monotonic relationships: Area vs World Pop %                  (0.841), Area vs Density (-0.584), Area vs Growth Rate (0.356).
      * Pearson underestimates these because of the extreme values (China, Russia,                   city-states like Macau and Singapore), which we deliberately retained.
      * Correlation does not imply causation.


### Step 4.5, part 2: Merge and relate population to CO2

The merge needs care. The assignment says to merge “on country name”, but names differ between datasets, so I join on the 3-letter code and then check what didn’t match.

```{r}
# Prepare the two datasets with only the columns we need
pop_2022 <- world_population %>%
  select(CCA3, country = `Country/Territory`, Continent, population_2022 = `2022 Population`)

co2_2019 <- co2_emisions %>%
  select(country_code, co2_2019 = `2019`)

# Inner join keeps only countries present in both datasets
merged_data <- pop_2022 %>%
  inner_join(co2_2019, by = c("CCA3" = "country_code"))

# How many countries matched, and how many were lost from each side?
nrow(merged_data)
anti_join(pop_2022, co2_2019, by = c("CCA3" = "country_code"))$country   # in population only
anti_join(co2_2019, pop_2022, by = c("country_code" = "CCA3"))$country_code  # in CO2 only

# Missing CO2 values in the merged data
sum(is.na(merged_data$co2_2019))
```
1. Twenty countries are in the population data only. They are small territories and dependencies (Anguilla, Guadeloupe, Jersey, Martinique...) plus Taiwan, Vatican City and Western Sahara. The World Bank CO2 data doesn’t report them, so losing them is expected and legitimate.

2. One code is in the CO2 data only: MNP. This one looks odd. “Northern Mariana Islands” is on the population-only list, and MNP is on the CO2-only list, so they are probably the same place with different codes. A quick check:

```{r}
# What code does each dataset use for the Northern Mariana Islands?
world_population %>%
  filter(`Country/Territory` == "Northern Mariana Islands") %>%
  select(CCA3, `Country/Territory`)

co2_emisions %>%
  filter(country_code == "MNP") %>%
  select(`Country Name`, country_code, `2019`)
```

```{r}
# Is Norfolk Island in the population data, and what code does it have?
world_population %>%
  filter(`Country/Territory` %in% c("Norfolk Island", "Northern Mariana Islands")) %>%
  select(CCA3, `Country/Territory`)

# Does the CO2 data contain NFK?
co2_emisions %>%
  filter(country_code == "NFK") %>%
  select(`Country Name`, country_code, `2019`)
```
```{r}
# Correct the mislabeled code so the country joins properly
# case_when() changes the code only for this country and leaves all others unchanged
world_population <- world_population %>%
  mutate(CCA3 = case_when(
    `Country/Territory` == "Northern Mariana Islands" ~ "MNP",
    TRUE ~ CCA3
  ))

# Confirm the change
world_population %>%
  filter(`Country/Territory` == "Northern Mariana Islands") %>%
  select(CCA3, `Country/Territory`)
```

```{r}
# Prepare the two datasets with only the columns we need
pop_2022 <- world_population %>%
  select(CCA3, country = `Country/Territory`, Continent, population_2022 = `2022 Population`)

co2_2019 <- co2_emisions %>%
  select(country_code, co2_2019 = `2019`)

# Inner join keeps only countries present in both datasets
merged_data <- pop_2022 %>%
  inner_join(co2_2019, by = c("CCA3" = "country_code"))

# Expected: 215 matched rows, 19 population-only territories, 0 CO2-only codes
nrow(merged_data)
anti_join(pop_2022, co2_2019, by = c("CCA3" = "country_code"))$country
anti_join(co2_2019, pop_2022, by = c("country_code" = "CCA3"))$country_code

# Expected: 24 missing 2019 values (the earlier 23 plus the Northern Mariana Islands)
sum(is.na(merged_data$co2_2019))
```


```{r}
# Matched countries with a missing 2019 CO2 value, largest populations first
merged_data %>%
  filter(is.na(co2_2019)) %>%
  select(country, Continent, population_2022) %>%
  arrange(desc(population_2022))

# Keep only countries that have both a 2022 population and a 2019 CO2 value
merged_complete <- merged_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(co2_2019))

nrow(merged_complete)   # expect 215 - 24 = 191
```



```{r}
# Pearson (linear) and Spearman (rank-based) correlations
cor(merged_complete$population_2022, merged_complete$co2_2019, method = "pearson")
cor(merged_complete$population_2022, merged_complete$co2_2019, method = "spearman")
```

Because the CO2 variable is per capita, the weak result is almost by construction. For a more meaningful view of population against emissions, created total emissions as a new variable (the assignment lists “creating new variables from existing ones” as an objective):

```{r}
# Total CO2 (metric tons) = per-capita emissions x population
# Note: mixes 2019 emissions with 2022 population, so it is an approximation
merged_complete <- merged_complete %>%
  mutate(total_co2 = co2_2019 * population_2022)

# Correlation between population and TOTAL emissions
cor(merged_complete$population_2022, merged_complete$total_co2, method = "pearson")
cor(merged_complete$population_2022, merged_complete$total_co2, method = "spearman")
```


### Step 4.6: CO2 emissions by continent
1. Sum 2019 CO2 by continent (as the assignment words it)

The assignment says to sum 2019 emissions by continent and report the result in metric tons per capita. I follow it literally: group_by() splits the data by continent, and summarise() collapses each group into one row.

```{r}
# Sum the 2019 per-capita CO2 values of the countries in each continent
# n() counts the countries, so we can see how many contribute to each sum
continent_co2 <- merged_complete %>%
  group_by(Continent) %>%
  summarise(countries           = n(),
            sum_co2_per_capita  = sum(co2_2019),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(sum_co2_per_capita))

continent_co2
```
```{r}
# Bar chart: reorder() sorts the bars, coord_flip() keeps the labels readable
ggplot(continent_co2,
       aes(x = reorder(Continent, sum_co2_per_capita),
           y = sum_co2_per_capita)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(sum_co2_per_capita, 1)), hjust = -0.1) +
  coord_flip() +
  expand_limits(y = max(continent_co2$sum_co2_per_capita) * 1.1) +  # room for the labels
  labs(title    = "Sum of 2019 CO2 emissions per capita by continent",
       subtitle = "Sum of country values (metric tons per capita)",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Sum of CO2 per capita (metric tons)") +
  theme_minimal()
```
# A caution about this method

Adding up per-capita values depends on how many countries a continent has. Africa has many countries, so its sum can look large even though each person emits little. For that reason, I also use a second, more meaningful measure to report next to the assignment’s version:

```{r}
# Total emissions in metric tons per continent (per-capita x population)
# Population-weighted average per capita = total emissions / total population
continent_co2_better <- merged_complete %>%
  group_by(Continent) %>%
  summarise(total_co2_tons       = sum(total_co2),
            total_population     = sum(population_2022),
            weighted_per_capita  = total_co2_tons / total_population,
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(total_co2_tons))

continent_co2_better
```

```{r}
# Scatter plot, both axes on a log scale
ggplot(merged_complete, aes(x = population_2022, y = co2_2019)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title    = "Population (2022) vs CO2 emissions per capita (2019)",
       subtitle = "Both axes on a log scale",
       x = "Population, 2022 (log scale)",
       y = "CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita, log scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```
```{r}
# Regression on the logged variables
co2_model <- lm(log10(co2_2019) ~ log10(population_2022), data = merged_complete)
summary(co2_model)
```
